questions.question: BrightCart's Jan cohort has 4 customers; only 1 of them placed an order in February (Month 1). What is the Month 1 retention rate for the Jan cohort?
questions.explanation: Month 1 retention = customers active in Month 1 / cohort size = 1/4 = 25%. This matches the lab's cohort matrix: of C01-C04, only C01 placed a delivered order in February.

questions.question: Why does the lab caution against concluding paid search is unprofitable after only 1-3 months of cohort data, even though the computed LTV:CAC ratio (0.375:1) is well below the 3:1 benchmark?
options: The math was done incorrectly

An immature cohort hasn't had time to repeat-purchase or fully reveal its lifetime value yet — judging a channel from early-tenure data is the same mistake as applying Month 1 churn to a lifetime LTV formula
CAC should never be compared to LTV
Paid search is always profitable regardless of the numbers
questions.explanation: This mirrors the ARPU/Churn Rate counterexample in the lesson: early-tenure behavior (high churn, low repeat purchases) is not representative of a cohort's mature, blended behavior. Cutting the channel based on 1-3 months of data risks killing a channel that would have been profitable on a 12-month view.

questions.question: Why must LTV be calculated using contribution margin (profit) rather than gross revenue?
options: Revenue is harder to calculate than profit
Using gross revenue overstates LTV because it ignores cost of goods, fulfillment, and payment processing — a customer who generates $200 in revenue might only generate $60 in actual profit
Profit and revenue are always the same number
Finance requires it for tax purposes only
questions.explanation: LTV is meant to answer 'how much can we afford to spend acquiring this customer?' That question can only be answered with profit (contribution margin), not top-line revenue — otherwise a company could mistakenly believe a money-losing acquisition channel is profitable.

questions.question: A SaaS company reports LTV:CAC of 5:1 (excellent) but has an 18-month payback period. What risk does the LTV:CAC ratio hide?
options: No risk — a 5:1 ratio is always safe regardless of payback period
The company could run out of cash before the value is realized, even though the long-run ratio looks great on paper
The ratio is mathematically impossible
Payback period is irrelevant to unit economics
questions.explanation: LTV:CAC describes eventual profitability but says nothing about cash flow timing. A long payback period means the company fronts the acquisition cost and waits a long time to recoup it — a real cash constraint that a high ratio alone doesn't reveal.

questions.question: BrightCart's overall conversion rate is flat year-over-year, but web, app, AND marketplace channels each individually improved. What's the most likely explanation, and what is this phenomenon called?
options: A calculation error; this is impossible
Simpson's Paradox — the customer mix shifted toward a lower-converting channel (e.g., marketplace) even though every individual channel improved
Survivorship bias
Goodhart's Law
questions.explanation: Simpson's Paradox occurs when a blended trend reverses or masks segment-level trends due to a shift in mix. If marketplace converts worse than web/app but grew fastest as a share of traffic, the blended average can stay flat even while every channel improved — a senior analyst should always check segment-level trends, not just the headline number.

questions.question: Why is measuring 'average satisfaction of current customers' prone to survivorship bias?
options: Current customers always lie on surveys
Customers who were dissatisfied and already churned are no longer in the sample, so the remaining base looks artificially satisfied regardless of real product quality
Survivorship bias only applies to historical stock market data
Surveys cannot measure satisfaction accurately
questions.explanation: If unhappy customers leave fastest, they exit the measurable population before they can report dissatisfaction. The survey of 'who's still here' systematically excludes the people most likely to report problems, inflating the apparent satisfaction score.

questions.question: BrightCart redefines 'Active Customer' to exclude marketplace buyers, and the historical chart suddenly shows a 30% drop. What is the correct senior-level response?
options: Report the 30% drop as a real business decline
Version the metric (e.g., v1 vs v2), document the change, and restate historical periods under the new definition so the trend line remains comparable
Delete the old chart and never mention the change
Ignore the discrepancy since it's just a dashboard
questions.explanation: A definition change is not a business change. Silently redefining a metric in place creates a false signal. Versioning the metric and restating history (with a changelog) preserves the integrity of trend analysis and prevents a stakeholder from mistaking a definitional artifact for an actual decline.

questions.question: What happens when you incentivize a single metric too aggressively, per Goodhart's Law?
options: Performance improves with no downside
People find ways to game the metric, often at the expense of the underlying goal it was meant to represent
The metric becomes impossible to measure
Nothing changes
questions.explanation: Goodhart's Law: 'when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' E.g., incentivizing low support call duration can cause agents to rush or hang up on difficult customers — the metric improves while the real goal (customer satisfaction) deteriorates. This is why guardrail metrics must accompany any north-star metric.
